canonical_statement: HOPE was a double-blind, randomized, two-by-two factorial trial evaluating ramipril and vitamin E.
Before randomization, 10,576 eligible patients completed a ramipril/placebo run-in; 1035 were excluded for noncompliance, side effects, abnormal creatinine or potassium, or withdrawal of consent.
Ramipril was titrated from 2.5 mg once daily for one week to 5 mg once daily for three weeks and then 10 mg once daily.

exposures.details: Titrated from 2.5 mg once daily for 1 week to 5 mg for 3 weeks, then 10 mg once daily.

canonical_statement: The control group received matching placebo.
Participants were also factorially randomized to vitamin E 400 IU daily or matching placebo.
Follow-up occurred at one month, six months, and every six months thereafter; primary and secondary events were centrally adjudicated using standardized definitions.
The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes.

concept.text: Myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death

canonical_statement: Death from any cause was a secondary outcome.
Revascularization was a secondary outcome.
Hospitalization for unstable angina was a secondary outcome.
Hospitalization for heart failure was a secondary outcome.
Complications related to diabetes was a secondary outcome.

outcome.definition: Diabetic nephropathy, renal dialysis, or laser therapy for diabetic retinopathy.

canonical_statement: Worsening angina was an additional prespecified outcome.
Cardiac arrest was an additional prespecified outcome.
Heart failure was an additional prespecified outcome.
Unstable angina with electrocardiographic changes was an additional prespecified outcome.
Development of diabetes was an additional prespecified outcome.
The primary analyses used intention-to-treat principles, Kaplan-Meier estimates, and log-rank comparisons, stratified for vitamin E randomization.
Subgroup analyses used interaction tests in Cox regression models stratified for vitamin E randomization.
The data and safety monitoring board recommended early termination on March 22, 1999 after repeated crossing of prespecified benefit boundaries for the primary outcome.
Vital status was ascertained for 9535 of 9541 randomized participants (99.9%) at the end of the study.
In the ramipril group, 65.0% were taking 10 mg daily at the last visit; placebo-group use of a nonstudy ACE inhibitor increased to 12.3% by five years.
Mean blood pressure at study end was 136/76 mm Hg with ramipril and 139/77 mm Hg with placebo.
Ramipril reduced the primary composite outcome to 14.0% versus 17.8% with placebo (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.70-0.86; P<0.001).

canonical_statement: Left ventricular function was not measured in all participants; a 496-patient substudy found ejection fraction below 0.40 in 2.6%, and chart review found low ejection fraction in 8.1% of 5193 participants whose ventricular function had been assessed before randomization.

The investigators concluded that ramipril reduced death, myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization, cardiac arrest, heart failure, diabetes-related complications, and new diabetes in a broad spectrum of high-risk patients.
The investigators reported reduced heart failure incidence in patients with no evidence of impairment of left ventricular systolic function.
The investigators estimated that treating 1000 patients with ramipril for four years prevents about 150 events in approximately 70 patients.
